title: One week into a 2D roguelite where AI writes every line of code and I make the design calls (13 years AAA design)
author: Luc1dJay
selftext:
I've designed games at AAA studios for 13 years. Last week I started my own game, Project Salvage Run (working title): a pixel art roguelite about a salvage diver keeping her stranded crew alive. My rule is that I make every design call and AI does the building. Here's how that's going after one week.

What the AI does:

\- Writes all the code (Godot 4, GDScript), opens a pull request for each feature, and builds Windows, Steam Deck and phone versions on every merge

\- Makes the art from scripts: pixel sprites from a code rig, and big set pieces modelled in Blender and painted down to a locked palette

\- A route bot replays every jump in the movement test level (74 sections), and a nightly audit runs the tests and checks the design wiki for contradictions

\- Cuts these dev diaries from real in-engine footage every night

What I do:

\- Every design decision (200 so far, all logged on a wiki), the feel tuning, and saying no a lot

What didn't work: AI sprite generators drifted between animation frames, so I dropped them. Sprites come from a scripted rig on a locked palette now.

The video shows the latest diary: shield levels, a hazard test room, parallax layers, and an open question. Pixel art or painted, which would you play?

https://www.instagram.com/small.scale.machine?exln=MThhejQwYXF2MDExNA==

Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
